newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sugar import quota doubts plague Russian industry.
newsitem.headline: Sugar import quota doubts plague Russian industry.

text.p: The fate of Russia's plan to slap quotas on refined sugar imports is unclear, and doubts over when or even if the curbs will come are casting a long shadow over the country's ailing sugar industry, traders said on Tuesday.
"It is impossible to know what will finally be decided at this stage," a sugar trader said.
"The question of imports is a big problem," another said. "Last year a huge amount of sugar came on to the Russian market, and this was one of the reasons for the fall in market prices."
Some industry officials were still confident the quota plan would succeed, promising it would give Russian refineries a much-needed boost after a difficult year in 1996.
"I think that there will definitely be a quota (on white sugar imports)," Vasily Severin, head of the Rossakhsvyokla sugar producers' association, said.
"Maybe it will be in a slightly different form (from the current proposal), but there will be some form of protection."
Last year the Foreign Trade Ministry sent an order to the government calling for white sugar imports to be limited to 1.5 million tonnes a year, including 1.15 million from Ukraine.
When asked to explain why the government had thus far failed to act upon the order, Severin said, "I think this is a normal procedural delay which needs further clarification."
Russian refineries are keen to process imported Cuban raws and to avoid Ukrainian and European competition.

Over the past 12 months Russian government officials have beaten a protectionist drum and called for measures to defend domestic food producers. But some cabinet officials have said non-tariff forms of regulation will not help Russia.
Ukrainian imports are already subject to a 10 percent value-added tax, introduced late in 1996.
Cheaper Ukrainian sugar swamped the Russian market in 1996, pushing prices down and forcing domestic sugar refiners to operate way below capacity.
"Last year Ukraine was very competitive with its operations in the Russian sugar industry, and the domestic (Russian) market was in very bad shape," a trader said.
A lack of consumer spending power and financial woes at sugar refineries have also pushed down demand, traders said, adding that the outlook for 1997 was little better.
"Consumption in Russia is still too low. This year it could be as low as 4.5 million tonnes," one trader said.
But Severin said demand was likely to be higher.
"On demand, I think it will be somewhere in the region of 5.0 to 5.5 million tonnes," he said.
However, this was still below his forecast of total Russian refined sugar supplies in 1997 of 6.0 million tonnes.
Russia's 1996 sugar beet harvest has been revised up slightly to 16.1 million tonnes from a previously estimated 16.0 million. Last year's output was 19.1 million tonnes.

Figures from the Russian State Statistics Committee show Russia imported 1.38 million tonnes of refined sugar from all countries during the first 11 months of 1996, down 12 percent from the same period in 1995.
